name: Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction
summary: Carboxylic acids having α-H are halogenated at the α-carbon by Cl2 or Br2 in the presence of red phosphorus; the acyl halide formed in situ enolises and is halogenated, then hydrolysed.
mechanism: Red P + Br2 gives PBr3, which converts RCOOH to RCOBr. The acyl bromide enolises readily and the enol attacks Br2 at the α-carbon to give α-bromoacyl bromide. Water (or exchange with more RCOOH) gives the α-bromo acid.
keyPoints: Needs at least one α-hydrogen (HCOOH and (CH3)3CCOOH do not react)
Only α-substitution; carbon chain is not touched
Excess halogen can give α,α-dihalo acids
α-Halo acid + NH3 gives α-amino acid (e.g. glycine, alanine)
whenUsed: Preparing α-halo acids, a route to α-hydroxy and α-amino acids.
jeeTips: Halogenation occurs at α-C, not β. Red P is essential; plain Br2 with acid gives no reaction. Often appears as a step: acid -> α-bromo acid -> amino acid / hydroxy acid.

name: Claisen Condensation
summary: Two molecules of an ester having α-H condense in the presence of a strong alkoxide base to give a β-keto ester.
mechanism: Ethoxide removes an α-H to give an ester enolate, which attacks the C=O of a second ester (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Loss of ethoxide gives the β-keto ester, which is deprotonated at the doubly activated CH2; this irreversible step drives the equilibrium.
keyPoints: Ester must have at least two α-H for good yield (the product needs an acidic α-H to be deprotonated)
Use the alkoxide matching the ester alkyl group (NaOEt for ethyl esters) to avoid transesterification
Crossed Claisen works if one ester has no α-H (e.g. ethyl benzoate, ethyl formate)
Final acidification liberates the β-keto ester
whenUsed: Synthesis of β-keto esters and 1,3-diketones (ketone + ester).
applications: Precursor to ketones via acetoacetic ester route
jeeTips: Product is a β-keto ester, not an aldol. A stoichiometric (not catalytic) amount of base is needed. Ester of type R2CHCOOEt (one α-H) fails to condense in the simple Claisen.

name: Dieckmann Condensation
summary: Intramolecular Claisen condensation of a 1,6- or 1,7-diester in base giving a cyclic β-keto ester (5- or 6-membered ring).
mechanism: Ethoxide forms an enolate at the α-carbon of one ester; it attacks the other ester carbonyl intramolecularly to form a five- or six-membered ring after loss of EtO-. The cyclic β-keto ester is deprotonated to drive the reaction.
keyPoints: Diethyl adipate (1,6-diester) gives a 5-membered ring; diethyl pimelate (1,7) gives a 6-membered ring
Rings smaller than 5 or larger than 7 form poorly
Hydrolysis and decarboxylation of the product gives a cyclic ketone
Needs an α-H on the new carbon bearing the ester for the driving deprotonation
whenUsed: Synthesis of cyclopentanone and cyclohexanone derivatives.
applications: Cyclic ketones after hydrolysis and decarboxylation
jeeTips: Count the carbons: adipic ester gives cyclopentanone, not cyclohexanone. Remember it is simply the intramolecular version of Claisen condensation.

name: Arndt–Eistert Homologation
summary: Converts a carboxylic acid into its next higher homologue by acid chloride -> diazoketone -> Wolff rearrangement to a ketene, trapped by water.
mechanism: RCOCl reacts with CH2N2 to give the diazoketone RCOCHN2 (2 equiv CH2N2 absorb the HCl). With Ag2O/H2O, N2 is lost and R migrates to the carbene carbon (Wolff rearrangement) to give ketene RCH=C=O, which adds water to give RCH2COOH.
keyPoints: Chain lengthened by exactly one carbon
Two equivalents of CH2N2 are used (one makes diazoketone, one removes HCl as CH3Cl)
Ketene intermediate; ROH gives ester, NH3 gives amide
Migrating group retains its configuration
whenUsed: Chain extension of acids, e.g. conversion of amino acids to β-amino acids.
jeeTips: Product has ONE more carbon than the starting acid. Key intermediate is the ketene, not an isocyanate (do not confuse with Curtius/Hofmann which lose carbon).

name: Schmidt Reaction (Carboxylic Acid to Amine)
productName: Primary amine with one carbon less
summary: A carboxylic acid reacts with hydrazoic acid in conc. H2SO4 to give a primary amine having one carbon atom less, with loss of CO2 and N2.
mechanism: Protonated RCOOH forms an acyl azide-like species (RCON3 / acylium + HN3). Loss of N2 with R migration from C to N gives the isocyanate RN=C=O, which is hydrolysed to the carbamic acid and then decarboxylated to RNH2.
keyPoints: Carbon count decreases by one
Ketones with HN3 give amides instead (Schmidt on ketones)
Same isocyanate pathway as Curtius, but done in one pot in strongly acidic medium
Migrating group keeps its configuration
whenUsed: Direct conversion of acids to amines without isolating an acyl azide.
applications: Preparation of aromatic amines from aromatic acids

examples.eq: CH3COOH + HN3 ->[conc. H2SO4] CH3NH2 + CO2 + N2
C6H5COOH + HN3 ->[conc. H2SO4] C6H5NH2 + CO2 + N2

jeeTips: Amine formed has one carbon less than the acid. Compare: Hofmann (amide + Br2/KOH), Curtius (acyl azide, heat), Schmidt (acid + HN3/H2SO4) all give the same RNH2.

name: Curtius Rearrangement
summary: An acyl azide, made from an acid chloride and NaN3, loses N2 on heating to give an isocyanate that is hydrolysed to a primary amine with one carbon less.
mechanism: Thermal loss of N2 from RCON3 is concerted with 1,2-shift of R from carbon to nitrogen, giving RN=C=O. Water adds to isocyanate to give an unstable carbamic acid, which loses CO2 to give RNH2. Alcohol instead of water traps the isocyanate as a carbamate (urethane).
keyPoints: RCOOH -> RCOCl -> RCON3 -> RN=C=O -> RNH2
Amine has one C less than the acid
Isocyanate can be isolated and trapped with ROH (carbamate) or amine (urea)
Retention of configuration of the migrating group
whenUsed: Clean preparation of primary amines from acids.
jeeTips: Intermediate is an isocyanate (R-N=C=O). Net: RCOOH -> RNH2 (loss of one C as CO2). Don't confuse with Wolff (carbon gained).

name: Lossen Rearrangement
summary: An O-acylated hydroxamic acid rearranges with base to an isocyanate, which is hydrolysed to a primary amine having one carbon less.
mechanism: Base removes the N–H proton of RCONH–OCOR'. The anion expels the carboxylate leaving group as R migrates from C to N, giving RN=C=O. Hydrolysis of the isocyanate gives RNH2 + CO2.
keyPoints: Starting material is hydroxamic acid derivative RCONHOH (O-acyl or O-sulfonyl)
Passes through isocyanate like Hofmann and Curtius
Amine has one carbon less than the acid derivative
Migrating group keeps configuration
whenUsed: Alternative degradation to amine when acyl azide or bromamide route is unsuitable.
jeeTips: Memorise the trio giving isocyanates: Hofmann (RCONH2), Curtius (RCON3), Lossen (RCONHOCOR'). All give RNH2 with one C less.

name: Acid Chloride Formation (SOCl2 / PCl5)
aliases: Conversion of acids to acyl chlorides
summary: Carboxylic acids are converted into acid chlorides by replacing OH with Cl using SOCl2, PCl5 or PCl3.
mechanism: The acid OH attacks sulphur (or phosphorus) to form an acyl chlorosulphite (or acyl-O-PCl4) leaving group. Chloride then attacks the carbonyl carbon and the leaving group departs as SO2 + Cl- (or POCl3).
keyPoints: SOCl2 is preferred: by-products SO2 and HCl are gases, pure product is left
PCl5 gives POCl3 + HCl; PCl3 gives H3PO3
Test for –OH group: PCl5 gives steamy fumes of HCl
Acid chlorides are the most reactive acid derivatives
whenUsed: Activation of acids for esters, amides, anhydrides and Friedel–Crafts acylation.
applications: Synthesis of Rosenmund and Arndt–Eistert intermediates
jeeTips: SOCl2 is best because by-products are gaseous. Phenol does NOT give aryl chloride with PCl5 cleanly. Formic acid does not give HCOCl (unstable).

name: Ester Hydrolysis / Saponification
summary: Esters are cleaved by water: reversibly in acid, and irreversibly in base (saponification) to give carboxylate salt and alcohol.
mechanism: Base: OH- attacks the ester C=O (BAC2) to form a tetrahedral intermediate that expels RO-; the acid formed is immediately deprotonated, making the reaction irreversible. Acid: protonated ester is attacked by H2O (AAC2), reversible, equilibrium shifted using excess water.
keyPoints: Base hydrolysis is irreversible and goes to completion
Acid hydrolysis is reversible (reverse of Fischer esterification)
Fats + NaOH gives soap + glycerol
Ester hydrolysis with H2(18O) puts 18O in the acid (acyl–oxygen cleavage)
whenUsed: Manufacture of soap, determination of ester saponification value.
jeeTips: Acid hydrolysis = equilibrium, base = complete. Mechanism cleaves acyl–O bond, not alkyl–O bond (except for tertiary esters in acid).

name: Transesterification
summary: An ester reacts with another alcohol in the presence of an acid or base catalyst to exchange its alkoxy group.
mechanism: Under base, RO- adds to the ester carbonyl giving a tetrahedral intermediate that expels the original alkoxide. Under acid, the protonated carbonyl is attacked by the new alcohol, followed by proton transfers and loss of the old alcohol. Equilibrium is shifted by excess of one alcohol or removal of the other.
keyPoints: Reversible; use large excess of the incoming alcohol
Industrial biodiesel: vegetable oil + CH3OH -> fatty acid methyl esters + glycerol
Use alkoxide matching the ester to avoid mixed products in Claisen
PET synthesis uses transesterification of dimethyl terephthalate with glycol
whenUsed: Biodiesel production, polyester manufacture (Terylene/PET).
jeeTips: It is an equilibrium; do not call it hydrolysis (no water is involved).

name: Dehydration of Amides to Nitriles
summary: Primary amides lose a molecule of water on heating with a strong dehydrating agent such as P4O10 to give nitriles.
mechanism: The amide oxygen attacks phosphorus to give an O-phosphorylated imidate; loss of a proton from N and elimination of the phosphate group (as P-O species) creates the C≡N triple bond.
keyPoints: Only primary amides (–CONH2) give nitriles
Reverse of nitrile hydrolysis
Alternatives: SOCl2, POCl3
Carbon count is unchanged
whenUsed: Laboratory preparation of nitriles from acids via amides.
jeeTips: Amide -> nitrile loses H2O; Hofmann on same amide loses a carbon (amine). Choose reagents carefully in conversion sequences.

name: Reduction of Carboxylic Acids with LiAlH4
summary: Carboxylic acids are reduced all the way to primary alcohols by LiAlH4 (or B2H6); NaBH4 does not reduce them.
mechanism: The acid first loses H2 giving the carboxylate. Hydride attacks the carboxylate carbon, then an aldehyde is formed via loss of an O–Al species; the aldehyde is reduced faster than the acid, giving the alkoxide, protonated on work-up to RCH2OH.
keyPoints: NaBH4 cannot reduce acids; LiAlH4 and B2H6 can
B2H6 selectively reduces –COOH in the presence of an ester or nitro group
Reaction cannot be stopped at the aldehyde stage
Esters also give 1° alcohols (two alcohols) with LiAlH4; amides give amines
whenUsed: Converting acids to alcohols.
jeeTips: LiAlH4 gives alcohol (never aldehyde) from acids. NaBH4 is inert towards acids/esters. B2H6 reduces –COOH faster than an ester.

name: Grignard Reagent + CO2 (Carboxylation)
productName: Carboxylic acid with one extra carbon
summary: Grignard reagents add to solid CO2 (dry ice) to give magnesium carboxylate, which on acidification gives a carboxylic acid with one more carbon than the alkyl halide.
mechanism: The nucleophilic carbon of R-MgX attacks the electrophilic carbon of CO2 to give RCOOMgX. Hydrolysis with dilute acid liberates RCOOH.
keyPoints: Acid has one carbon more than R–X used
Works for primary, secondary, tertiary and aryl halides
Reagent must be prepared in dry ether; CO2 is used as dry ice
Suitable for making 3° acids, which cannot be made by SN2 with CN-
whenUsed: Chain-lengthening synthesis of acids from halides.
jeeTips: RX -> RMgX -> RCOOH adds one carbon. Moist ether or acidic H (OH, NH, terminal alkyne) destroys the Grignard.

name: Hydrolysis of Nitriles to Carboxylic Acids
summary: Nitriles are hydrolysed through the amide to carboxylic acids with aqueous acid or alkali, with loss of NH3 (NH4+).
mechanism: Water adds across the C≡N (after protonation or attack by OH-) to form an imidic acid that tautomerises to the amide. The amide is then hydrolysed to acid and NH3/NH4+. Partial hydrolysis (H2O2/OH- or conc. H2SO4, mild) can stop at the amide.
keyPoints: Carbon count same as nitrile; RX + KCN -> RCN -> RCOOH adds one carbon over RX
In alkali, the carboxylate salt is obtained and NH3 is evolved
Intermediate amide can be isolated under controlled conditions
Used for hydrolysis of cyanohydrins to α-hydroxy acids
whenUsed: Chain extension of halides by one carbon; synthesis of hydroxy acids.
jeeTips: Alkyl halide to acid with ONE extra carbon via CN-. Aryl halides do not react with KCN, so benzonitrile is made from the diazonium route instead.

name: Acetylation (Acid Chloride / Anhydride + Alcohol or Amine)
summary: Replacement of active H of –OH, –NH2 by an acetyl group using acetyl chloride or acetic anhydride, to give esters and amides.
mechanism: Nucleophilic acyl substitution: the lone pair of N or O adds to the acyl carbon to form a tetrahedral intermediate, then Cl- (or acetate) leaves. Pyridine removes the HCl formed and shifts equilibrium.
keyPoints: Reactivity order: acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide
Acetylation of aniline protects the NH2 group (lowers its activating strength)
Salicylic acid + (CH3CO)2O gives aspirin
Base (pyridine) is needed to neutralise HCl
whenUsed: Protection of amino groups, synthesis of aspirin, esters and amides.
jeeTips: 3° amines do not get acylated (no N–H). Acylation needs a base; Friedel–Crafts acylation is different (C-acylation of arene).

name: Sodium Bicarbonate Test for Carboxylic Acids
summary: Carboxylic acids (pKa about 4–5) are strong enough to decompose sodium bicarbonate with brisk effervescence of CO2; phenols (pKa about 10) do not.
mechanism: Proton transfer from RCOOH to HCO3- gives carbonic acid, which breaks down to H2O and CO2 gas. The CO2 turns lime water milky.
keyPoints: Positive for –COOH, also for sulphonic acids and strongly acidic phenols like picric acid
Phenol, alcohols, ketones: no CO2
Distinguishes benzoic acid from phenol
Effervescence tested with lime water
whenUsed: Quick distinction between acids and phenols.
jeeTips: Phenol is a weaker acid than H2CO3, so no CO2. 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid) does give CO2. Phenols react with NaOH but not NaHCO3.

name: Malonic Ester Synthesis
summary: Diethyl malonate is deprotonated, alkylated, hydrolysed and decarboxylated to give mono- or di-substituted acetic acids.
mechanism: The active methylene (pKa ≈ 13) is removed by ethoxide to give a stabilised enolate, which attacks R–X in an SN2 step. Ester hydrolysis gives the substituted malonic acid, whose β-carboxyl is lost as CO2 on heating through a cyclic six-membered transition state.
keyPoints: Product: R–CH2–COOH (one alkyl) or R2CH–COOH (two alkylations)
Use primary alkyl halides (SN2); tertiary and aryl halides fail
Net: RX is converted to RCH2COOH (two carbons added)
With dihalides gives cyclic acids (e.g. 1,2-dibromoethane -> cyclopropane carboxylic acid)
whenUsed: Preparation of substituted acetic acids and cycloalkane carboxylic acids.
jeeTips: With RX you get RCH2COOH (not RCOOH). Aryl halides and 3° halides cannot be used. Dialkylation yields R2CHCOOH.

name: Acetoacetic Ester Synthesis
reagents: (i) NaOEt; (ii) RX; (iii) dil. NaOH / H3O+, heat
summary: Ethyl acetoacetate is alkylated at the active methylene and then hydrolysed and decarboxylated (ketonic hydrolysis) to give a methyl ketone.
mechanism: Ethoxide forms the stabilised enolate (pKa ≈ 11), which is alkylated by RX (SN2). Dilute alkali hydrolysis followed by acidification gives the β-keto acid, which decarboxylates on warming to a ketone. Concentrated alkali instead causes acid cleavage to give acids.
keyPoints: Ketonic hydrolysis (dilute NaOH): gives ketone
Acid hydrolysis (conc. NaOH): gives two molecules of acids
Final ketone is CH3COCH2R (monoalkyl) or CH3COCHR2
Use 1° halides; two successive alkylations possible
whenUsed: Synthesis of methyl ketones, γ-diketones and keto acids.

examples.eq: CH3COCH(CH3)COOC2H5 ->[\text{1. dil. NaOH}][\text{2. }H3O+,\Delta] CH3COCH2CH3 + CO2 + C2H5OH

jeeTips: Dilute base gives ketone, conc. base gives acids (acid hydrolysis). Product ketone always carries CH3CO– unit.

name: Decarboxylation of β-Keto Acids
summary: β-Keto acids (and malonic acids) lose CO2 readily on gentle heating via a cyclic six-membered transition state to give a ketone (or monocarboxylic acid).
mechanism: The carboxyl H is transferred to the β-carbonyl O through a six-membered cyclic transition state while the C–C bond breaks and CO2 is lost, giving an enol which tautomerises to the ketone.
keyPoints: Needs a carbonyl at the β-position (3-oxo) to the COOH
Malonic acid: HOOCCH2COOH -> CH3COOH + CO2 on heating
Cyclic TS and enol intermediate
Bridgehead β-keto acids do not decarboxylate (Bredt's rule; enol cannot form)
whenUsed: Final step of malonic and acetoacetic ester syntheses.
jeeTips: Simple acids such as CH3COOH do not decarboxylate by heat alone; they need soda lime (NaOH/CaO). β-Keto acids lose CO2 at moderate temperature.

name: Hofmann Bromamide Degradation
productName: Primary amine with one carbon less
summary: A primary amide reacts with Br2 in aqueous KOH (or NaOBr) to give a primary amine containing one carbon atom less than the amide.
mechanism: The amide is N-brominated to RCONHBr, deprotonated to the bromoamide anion. R migrates from C to N with loss of Br- to give the isocyanate RN=C=O. Hydrolysis gives carbamate and then RNH2 + CO3 2-.
keyPoints: Amine has one C less than the amide
Migrating group retains configuration (optically active R gives optically active amine)
Only primary amides
Gives pure 1° amine, with no 2°/3° contaminant
whenUsed: Preparing pure primary amines (including aromatic amines such as aniline).

examples.eq: CH3CONH2 + Br2 + 4 KOH -> CH3NH2 + K2CO3 + 2 KBr + 2 H2O
C6H5CONH2 + Br2 + 4 KOH -> C6H5NH2 + K2CO3 + 2 KBr + 2 H2O

jeeTips: Always one C less. Intermediate: isocyanate. Questions may ask the number of moles of KOH (4) — total equation: RCONH2 + Br2 + 4KOH. Don't confuse with Gabriel (same carbon count).

name: Gabriel Phthalimide Synthesis
summary: Potassium phthalimide, an N-nucleophile, is alkylated by a primary alkyl halide; hydrolysis (or hydrazinolysis) frees the pure primary amine.
mechanism: KOH deprotonates phthalimide (pKa ≈ 8.3) to give the nucleophilic phthalimide anion, which displaces halide from R–X by SN2. The N-alkylphthalimide is hydrolysed with aq. NaOH (or N2H4) to RNH2 and phthalate (or phthalhydrazide).
keyPoints: Gives ONLY primary amines (no 2° or 3°)
Works with primary alkyl halides; fails with aryl halides (no SN2) and with tertiary halides (elimination)
Aromatic primary amines cannot be made
Carbon count same as RX
whenUsed: Clean laboratory synthesis of aliphatic primary amines.
jeeTips: Cannot prepare aniline by Gabriel. Product is always 1° amine only. Compare with Hofmann ammonolysis (mixture).

name: Carbylamine (Isocyanide) Test
summary: Only primary amines (aliphatic or aromatic) on warming with chloroform and alcoholic KOH give isocyanides (carbylamines) with an extremely offensive smell.
mechanism: KOH generates dichlorocarbene (:CCl2) from CHCl3 by α-elimination. The nucleophilic NH2 attacks :CCl2, and two successive eliminations of HCl by KOH give the isocyanide R–N≡C.
keyPoints: Positive only for primary amines
2° and 3° amines give no foul smell
Used to detect 1° amino groups, also in aniline
Intermediate: dichlorocarbene
whenUsed: Qualitative test for 1° amines.

examples.eq: CH3NH2 + CHCl3 + 3 KOH -> CH3NC + 3 KCl + 3 H2O
C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + 3 KOH -> C6H5NC + 3 KCl + 3 H2O

jeeTips: Works with aniline too (unlike Hinsberg-type sulphonamide solubility trick). Amides do not give the test. The foul smell is the observation.

name: Hinsberg Test
summary: Benzenesulphonyl chloride distinguishes 1°, 2° and 3° amines: 1° gives a sulphonamide soluble in alkali, 2° gives an insoluble one, 3° does not react.
mechanism: The amine N attacks sulphur of C6H5SO2Cl with loss of Cl-. With 1° amines the N–H of the product is acidic (strongly electron-withdrawing SO2Ph group) and dissolves in KOH as the potassium salt. With 2° amines no N–H remains so the sulphonamide is insoluble.
keyPoints: 1° amine: sulphonamide soluble in KOH; on acidification it re-precipitates
2° amine: insoluble precipitate in KOH
3° amine: no reaction; remains insoluble amine, soluble in dilute HCl
Reagent also called Hinsberg reagent
whenUsed: Separation and identification of 1°, 2°, 3° amines.
jeeTips: Do not say 'in alkali 1° is insoluble'. 1° = soluble, 2° = insoluble, 3° = no reaction. Basic strength reasoning: N–H acidity from SO2Ph.

name: Hofmann Exhaustive Methylation and Elimination
summary: An amine is exhaustively methylated to a quaternary ammonium iodide, converted to the hydroxide with moist Ag2O, and then pyrolysed to give the least substituted alkene.
mechanism: Excess CH3I converts the amine to R–N+(CH3)3 I-. Ag2O/H2O replaces I- by OH-. On heating, E2 elimination takes place with OH- removing the most acidic, least hindered β-H (bulky leaving group), forming the less substituted alkene (Hofmann rule).
keyPoints: Gives least substituted alkene (Hofmann product), opposite to Saytzeff
Number of CH3I equivalents consumed identifies the type of amine (1°: 3, 2°: 2, 3°: 1)
Bulky NMe3 leaving group and acidity of H cause the regiochemistry
Used for structure determination of alkaloids
whenUsed: Structure elucidation of amines and alkaloids; making terminal alkenes.

examples.eq: CH3CH2CH2N+(CH3)3 I- ->[\text{Ag2O, H2O}] CH3CH2CH2N+(CH3)3 OH- + AgI

jeeTips: Hofmann product = LESS substituted alkene; Saytzeff with haloalkanes gives MORE substituted. Ag2O supplies OH-.

name: Mendius Reduction
aliases: Reduction of nitriles to primary amines
summary: Nitriles are reduced to primary amines by sodium and alcohol (nascent hydrogen); catalytic hydrogenation or LiAlH4 also work.
mechanism: Successive addition of hydrogen across the C≡N triple bond: first to imine RCH=NH (via electron transfer from Na and protonation by ethanol), then to RCH2NH2.
keyPoints: Carbon count unchanged between nitrile and amine; amine has one more C than R–X used to make RCN
Gives only primary amine
LiAlH4 or H2/Ni are alternatives; DIBAL-H gives aldehyde
Isocyanides give 2° amines (RNHCH3) on reduction instead
whenUsed: Preparation of primary amines with one extra carbon from alkyl halide.
applications: RX -> RCN -> RCH2NH2 chain-extension of amines
jeeTips: Nitrile gives 1° amine; isocyanide gives 2° N-methyl amine; do not mix up. Use of KCN then reduction adds one carbon (vs Gabriel which does not).

name: Reduction of Nitrobenzene to Aniline (Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl)
aliases: Reduction of nitro compounds in acidic medium
summary: Nitrobenzene is completely reduced to aniline (via nitroso and hydroxylamine) in strongly acidic medium by metals like Sn, Fe with HCl, or by catalytic hydrogenation.
mechanism: Six electrons (and six protons) are transferred: ArNO2 -> ArNO -> ArNHOH -> ArNH2. In HCl, Ar–NHOH is protonated and quickly reduced, so it does not accumulate or condense with nitroso compounds.
keyPoints: Sn/HCl or Fe/HCl: aniline is isolated as the anilinium salt, free amine with NaOH
Fe/HCl (with little HCl; FeCl2 regenerates acid) is the industrial route
Catalytic H2/Pd or Ni also gives aniline
Aromatic nitro group is reduced selectively with Sn/HCl, even in presence of C=O of some ketones
whenUsed: Principal route to aniline and aromatic amines.
applications: Manufacture of aniline, dyes and drugs (paracetamol)

examples.eq: C6H5NO2 + 3 H2 ->[\text{Ni or Pd}] C6H5NH2 + 2 H2O

jeeTips: Acidic medium always gives amine. Without work-up with base the product is C6H5NH3+ Cl-. m-Dinitrobenzene with (NH4)2S selectively gives m-nitroaniline (Zinin).

name: Reduction of Nitrobenzene in Neutral and Alkaline Media
summary: The product from nitrobenzene depends on the medium: neutral gives phenylhydroxylamine, mildly alkaline gives azoxybenzene, more strongly alkaline azobenzene and then hydrazobenzene; strongly acidic gives aniline.
mechanism: Stepwise reduction gives PhNO and PhNHOH. In neutral medium PhNHOH accumulates. In alkaline medium PhNO and PhNHOH condense (bimolecular reduction) to form azoxybenzene, which is progressively reduced to azobenzene and hydrazobenzene.
keyPoints: Neutral (Zn, NH4Cl): C6H5NHOH (N-phenylhydroxylamine)
Alkaline, mild (Na3AsO3 or NaOH, glucose): azoxybenzene C6H5N(O)=NC6H5
Alkaline (Zn, NaOH): azobenzene then hydrazobenzene
Hydrazobenzene in acid gives benzidine (benzidine rearrangement)
whenUsed: Preparation of azo/hydrazo compounds and benzidine.
jeeTips: Memorise medium -> product: acidic -> aniline; neutral -> phenylhydroxylamine; alkaline -> azoxy -> azo -> hydrazo. Hydrazobenzene + H+ gives benzidine.

name: Ammonolysis of Alkyl Halides (Hofmann Ammonolysis)
productName: Mixture of 1°, 2°, 3° amines and quaternary salt
summary: Alkyl halides react with ammonia in a sealed tube to give a mixture of primary, secondary, tertiary amines and the quaternary ammonium salt through repeated SN2 reactions.
mechanism: NH3 attacks R–X by SN2 to give RNH3+ X-, which is deprotonated by excess NH3 to RNH2. The more nucleophilic amines react again with R–X successively until the quaternary salt forms.
keyPoints: Product is a mixture; excess NH3 favours the primary amine
Reactivity of halides: RI > RBr > RCl
Basicity (aqueous): 2° > 3° > 1° (alkyl), ordering depends on R
Separation of mixture by fractional distillation or Hinsberg reagent
whenUsed: Preparation of aliphatic amines (poor selectivity).
jeeTips: Gives a mixture. For pure 1° amine use Gabriel or Hofmann bromamide. Aryl halides do not undergo ammonolysis under normal conditions.

name: Diazotisation
summary: A primary aromatic amine reacts with nitrous acid (NaNO2 + HCl) at 0–5 °C to give an arenediazonium salt.
mechanism: HNO2 (from NaNO2 + HCl) gives NO+ (nitrosonium). The amine N attacks NO+ to form an N-nitrosoammonium ion, which loses H+ to give the N-nitrosamine, tautomerises to diazohydroxide and, with acid, loses water to give Ar–N2+.
keyPoints: Must be kept at 0–5 °C: above this the diazonium salt hydrolyses to phenol and N2
Aliphatic 1° amines give unstable diazonium salts (alcohols + N2)
Diazonium salt is stabilised by resonance with the aryl ring
Used in situ; solid diazonium salts are explosive (except BF4-)
whenUsed: First step to prepare many aryl derivatives (Cl, Br, CN, I, F, OH, H, azo dyes).

examples.eq: C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2 HCl ->[\text{273-278 K}] C6H5N2+ Cl- + NaCl + 2 H2O
C6H5N2+ Cl- ->[\text{H2O, warm}] C6H5OH + N2 + HCl

jeeTips: Temperature 0–5 °C. NaNO2 + HCl generates HNO2 in situ (HNO2 is unstable). Aliphatic amines: no stable diazonium salt.

name: Sandmeyer Reaction
reagents: CuCl / HCl (or CuBr / HBr, CuCN / KCN)
summary: The diazonium group is replaced by Cl, Br or CN by treating the diazonium salt with the corresponding cuprous salt (CuCl, CuBr, CuCN).
mechanism: Single electron transfer from Cu(I) to Ar–N2+ gives Ar• + N2 and Cu(II). The aryl radical abstracts halide (or CN) from the Cu(II) species to give Ar–X and regenerates Cu(I) (radical chain).
keyPoints: Reagents are Cu(I) salts in the corresponding acid (CuCl/HCl, CuBr/HBr, CuCN/KCN)
Benzonitrile can be hydrolysed to benzoic acid
Radical mechanism
Fluoro and iodo compounds are not made this way (Balz–Schiemann, KI)
whenUsed: Introduction of Cl, Br, CN into the ring at positions where direct substitution fails.
applications: Benzoic acid from aniline via nitrile
jeeTips: Sandmeyer = Cu(I) salt in solution; Gattermann = Cu powder + HX. Sandmeyer gives higher yield. CuCN gives nitrile only (CN, not isocyanide).

name: Gattermann Reaction (Cu / HX)
summary: Diazonium salts are converted to aryl chlorides or bromides by warming with copper powder and the corresponding halogen acid (HCl or HBr).
mechanism: Copper powder (Cu0) transfers an electron to the diazonium ion giving an aryl radical and N2; the radical combines with halide from the Cu(I)X species formed.
keyPoints: Uses Cu powder and HX, whereas Sandmeyer uses CuX
Yield is lower than in the Sandmeyer reaction
Not to be confused with Gattermann–Koch formylation (CO + HCl, AlCl3)
Gives halides from diazonium salts, not from aromatic rings
whenUsed: Alternative to Sandmeyer to prepare aryl chlorides/bromides.
jeeTips: Cu/HX = Gattermann; CuX/HX = Sandmeyer. Gattermann–Koch (CO, HCl, anhyd. AlCl3/CuCl) gives benzaldehyde — a different reaction.

name: Balz–Schiemann Reaction
summary: An arenediazonium chloride is treated with fluoroboric acid to give the insoluble diazonium tetrafluoroborate, which on heating decomposes to the aryl fluoride, BF3 and N2.
mechanism: Ar–N2+ BF4- is isolated as a stable solid. On heating, N2 is lost to give aryl cation (or ion pair) that abstracts F- from BF4-, giving Ar–F and BF3.
keyPoints: Only practical method for aryl fluorides (direct fluorination too violent)
Diazonium tetrafluoroborate is isolable and stable
By-products: BF3 and N2
Diazonium BF4- on heating with NaNO2/Cu gives nitrobenzene (nitro replacement)
whenUsed: Making fluoroarenes for medicinal chemistry.

examples.eq: C6H5N2+ Cl- + HBF4 -> C6H5N2+ BF4- + HCl
C6H5N2+ BF4- ->[\text{NaNO2, Cu, }\Delta] C6H5NO2 + N2 + BF3

jeeTips: Fluorine from HBF4, not from KF/CuF. Aryl iodide from KI, aryl fluoride from HBF4 — popular pair for matching.

name: Replacement of Diazo Group by Hydrogen (H3PO2 / C2H5OH)
aliases: Hypophosphorous acid reduction of diazonium salt
summary: Mild reducing agents like hypophosphorous acid or ethanol replace the diazonium group by hydrogen, thereby removing the amino group from the ring.
mechanism: Radical pathway: H3PO2 (or ethanol) acts as H-atom donor to the aryl radical/cation formed on loss of N2, giving Ar–H. Ethanol is oxidised to acetaldehyde, H3PO2 to H3PO3.
keyPoints: Used to remove NH2 after it has directed other substituents
Ethanol also converts diazonium to arene, but may give ether (ArOEt) as by-product
Useful for making 1,3,5-tribromobenzene from aniline
Replaces N2+ by H, not by OH
whenUsed: Synthesis of meta-substituted or 1,3,5-trisubstituted benzenes impossible by direct substitution.

examples.eq: C6H5N2+ Cl- + H3PO2 + H2O -> C6H6 + N2 + H3PO3 + HCl
C6H5N2+ Cl- + CH3CH2OH -> C6H6 + N2 + CH3CHO + HCl

jeeTips: Key trick: use NH2 as a temporary activating/directing group, then remove with H3PO2. Ethanol gives acetaldehyde in the process.

name: Diazonium Salt to Phenol (Warm Water)
conditions: warm (above 283 K), or dil. H2SO4 heat
summary: On warming with water (or boiling with dilute H2SO4), arenediazonium salts are hydrolysed to phenols with evolution of N2.
mechanism: Loss of N2 gives the very unstable aryl cation (SN1-type), which is captured by water. Loss of proton from the oxonium ion gives ArOH.
keyPoints: Reaction is the reason diazotisation must be done at 0–5 °C
Strong acid (dil. H2SO4) minimises coupling of phenol with undecomposed diazonium salt
Aryl cation is highly reactive (no resonance stabilisation by π system)
Used to prepare phenols where substitution is impossible
whenUsed: Laboratory synthesis of phenols and substituted phenols.

examples.eq: C6H5N2+ Cl- + H2O ->[\text{warm}] C6H5OH + N2 + HCl
C6H5NH2 ->[\text{1. NaNO2, HCl, 273 K}][\text{2. H2O, }\Delta] C6H5OH

jeeTips: If phenol is formed in presence of diazonium salt it can couple to give azo dyes — use acid and warm to avoid this. Nitrogen gas evolves.

name: Diazonium Salt to Iodobenzene (KI)
summary: Replacing the diazonium group by iodine needs only aqueous KI; no copper catalyst is required.
mechanism: I- is a good enough reducing agent/nucleophile: electron transfer to Ar–N2+ gives Ar• + I•, N2 is lost and Ar–I forms (or direct nucleophilic displacement of N2).
keyPoints: No Cu catalyst needed (unlike Cl, Br, CN)
Direct iodination of benzene with I2 is reversible and fails; this route is used instead
Iodine is not introduced by Sandmeyer's CuI
Evolves N2 gas
whenUsed: Synthesis of aryl iodides.

examples.eq: C6H5N2+ Cl- + KI -> C6H5I + N2 + KCl
C6H5NH2 ->[\text{1. NaNO2, HCl, 273 K}][\text{2. KI}] C6H5I

jeeTips: Remember: Cl/Br/CN need Cu(I); F needs HBF4; I needs only KI.

name: Diazonium Coupling with Aniline (Aminoazobenzene)
summary: Benzenediazonium chloride couples with aniline at the para position in weakly acidic medium to give p-aminoazobenzene, a yellow azo dye.
mechanism: The diazonium ion is a weak electrophile and attacks the electron-rich para position of aniline (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Loss of H+ gives the azo compound, Ar–N=N–Ar', which has an extended conjugated chromophore (colour).
keyPoints: pH 4–5 (weakly acidic) for amines; pH 9–10 (mildly alkaline) for phenols
Para position attacked; ortho if para is blocked
–N=N– (azo) group is the chromophore
Product is yellow; with 2-naphthol an orange-red dye is formed
whenUsed: Azo dyes and indicators (methyl orange).
jeeTips: Coupling with phenols in alkaline medium, with amines in weakly acidic medium. Para position preferred. Product always has –N=N–.

name: Schotten–Baumann Reaction
summary: Amines (or phenols/alcohols) react with benzoyl chloride in the presence of aqueous NaOH or pyridine to give N-benzoyl amides or benzoate esters.
mechanism: Nucleophilic attack of the amine N (or phenoxide O) at the carbonyl of C6H5COCl gives a tetrahedral intermediate; chloride is expelled. The base neutralises HCl and drives the reaction forward.
keyPoints: Base removes HCl (shifts equilibrium) and prevents amine protonation
Works with 1° and 2° amines, phenols and alcohols; 3° amines do not form amides
Product from aniline: benzanilide (N-phenylbenzamide)
Used to prepare crystalline derivatives for identification
whenUsed: Protection of –NH2 and –OH and for preparing esters/amides.
jeeTips: Benzoylation = Schotten–Baumann (benzoyl chloride + NaOH). Acetylation uses acetyl chloride/acetic anhydride + pyridine. 3° amines do not react.

name: Nitrous Acid Test for 1°, 2° and 3° Amines
summary: Nitrous acid distinguishes amine classes: aliphatic 1° gives N2 gas and alcohol; 2° gives a yellow oily N-nitrosamine; 3° gives a soluble nitrite salt; aromatic 1° gives a diazonium salt.
mechanism: 1° aliphatic: unstable diazonium salt decomposes (N2 + carbocation + products). 2°: N attacks NO+ and loses H+, giving stable R2N–N=O. 3°: no N–H to lose, so only protonation (salt) or ring nitrosation (aromatic 3°, e.g. p-nitroso-N,N-dimethylaniline, green).
keyPoints: Aliphatic 1° amine: brisk effervescence of N2 + alcohol
Aromatic 1° amine: diazonium salt at 273–278 K (couples with 2-naphthol to give red dye)
2° amine (aliphatic or aromatic): yellow oily nitrosamine (Liebermann)
3° aliphatic: dissolves as R3NH+ NO2-; 3° aromatic: ring nitrosation, green solid
whenUsed: Qualitative separation of 1°, 2° and 3° amines.
jeeTips: 1° aliphatic gives N2 (effervescence); 1° aromatic gives diazonium at 0–5 °C (no gas), then coupling test. Don't write nitrosamine for 1° amines.

name: Azo Dye Test (Coupling with 2-Naphthol)
summary: Aromatic primary amines are diazotised at 0–5 °C and the cold solution is added to alkaline 2-naphthol; a brilliant orange-red azo dye precipitates.
mechanism: ArNH2 gives Ar–N2+ (diazotisation). The electrophilic diazonium ion couples with the electron-rich 1-position of the 2-naphthoxide ion (electrophilic aromatic substitution), giving the azo dye.
keyPoints: Positive only for aromatic primary amines
Aliphatic 1° amines give no dye (diazonium decomposes)
Alkaline medium needed for naphthoxide
Dye colour due to extended conjugation of –N=N–
whenUsed: Confirmatory test for aromatic primary amino group.

examples.eq: C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2 HCl -> C6H5N2+ Cl- + NaCl + 2 H2O
C6H5N2+ Cl- + C10H7O- Na+ -> C6H5-N=N-C10H6OH + NaCl

jeeTips: Test positive for aniline but NOT for CH3NH2. Always cold (273–278 K); coupling with phenol gives yellow/orange-yellow dyes, naphthol gives red-orange.

name: Bromination of Aniline (2,4,6-Tribromoaniline) and Protection via Acetanilide
summary: Aniline is so strongly activated that bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline at once; to make p-bromoaniline the NH2 group is first acetylated (acetanilide), brominated, then hydrolysed.
mechanism: The lone pair on N is delocalised into the ring (+M), strongly activating o- and p-positions for electrophilic substitution. In acetanilide the lone pair is also delocalised on the C=O, so activation is moderated, leaving mainly para substitution (steric hindrance reduces ortho).
keyPoints: Aniline + Br2/H2O: white ppt of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline, no catalyst needed
Protection: aniline -> acetanilide -> p-bromoacetanilide -> p-bromoaniline
Acetylation reduces activation and prevents oxidation
Test used to detect aniline
whenUsed: Preparing monobromoanilines and controlling reactivity.
jeeTips: Without protection you cannot stop at mono-bromo. Acetyl group is a weaker activator; major product para. Order: protect -> brominate -> deprotect.

name: Nitration of Aniline (Meta via Anilinium, Para via Acetanilide)
summary: Direct nitration of aniline gives a mixture with large meta product (anilinium ion is meta-directing) and tarry oxidation products; protection as acetanilide gives mainly p-nitroaniline.
mechanism: In the strongly acidic nitrating mixture aniline is protonated to anilinium, –NH3+, which is strongly deactivating and meta-directing. Unprotonated aniline reacts at o/p. Acetanilide is not protonated, and the amide N still activates o/p positions, with para dominant for steric reasons.
keyPoints: Direct nitration: significant (~47%) meta-nitroaniline along with para and tar
Protect by acetylation: aniline -> acetanilide -> p-nitroacetanilide -> p-nitroaniline
Also protects NH2 from oxidation by HNO3
Anilinium ion: –NH3+ is –I, meta director
whenUsed: Preparing p-nitroaniline selectively; understanding substituent effects.
jeeTips: Famous trap: aniline is o/p-directing, yet direct nitration gives about 47 percent meta due to anilinium. Use acetanilide for para. m-Nitroaniline is better made by partial reduction of m-dinitrobenzene.

name: Sulphonation of Aniline (Sulphanilic Acid, Zwitterion)
summary: Aniline heated with conc. H2SO4 at 453–473 K forms anilinium hydrogen sulphate which rearranges on heating to p-aminobenzenesulphonic acid (sulphanilic acid), existing as a dipolar ion.
mechanism: Aniline + H2SO4 gives anilinium hydrogen sulphate. On heating, dehydration and rearrangement by electrophilic sulphonation (SO3 attack) at para position gives sulphanilic acid. The –NH2 proton transfers to –SO3H to give the zwitterion H3N+–C6H4–SO3-.
keyPoints: Para product is formed on strong heating (thermodynamic)
Sulphanilic acid exists as a zwitterion (inner salt)
It has high melting point and is poorly soluble in organic solvents; insoluble in water but soluble in alkali
Diazotised sulphanilic acid is used to make methyl orange
whenUsed: Dye manufacture (methyl orange), sulpha drugs (via sulphanilamide).
jeeTips: Para-sulphonic acid, existing as a zwitterion (dipolar ion), hence high m.p. and low solubility in organic solvents. Not meta, despite anilinium intermediate.

name: Reductive Amination
summary: A carbonyl compound reacts with ammonia or an amine to form an imine/iminium that is reduced in situ (H2/Ni or NaBH3CN) to a 1°, 2° or 3° amine.
mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of NH3 (or RNH2/R2NH) to C=O gives a hemiaminal which loses water to give an imine (or iminium). The C=N is then reduced by H2/Ni or hydride (NaBH3CN, which selectively reduces C=N over C=O).
keyPoints: NH3 gives 1° amine; 1° amine gives 2°; 2° amine gives 3°
NaBH3CN reduces iminium ion faster than C=O, enabling one-pot reaction
Ketones give α-branched amines (e.g. acetone + NH3 -> isopropylamine)
Avoids poly-alkylation seen in ammonolysis
whenUsed: Clean synthesis of substituted amines from carbonyl compounds.
jeeTips: Carbon skeleton unchanged: the C=O carbon becomes CH–N. Choose the carbonyl and amine partners carefully for 2° and 3° amine targets.
